Nothing gives more pleasure than hearing the unmistakable growl of the mighty Rolls-Royce Merlin V12 supercharged piston engine, and then looking heavenward to see the beauty of elliptical wings as this historic masterpiece flies into clouds. Protector of our freedom, this legendary fighter plane is our heritage. In our S2 limited edition watch we have paid our own tribute to this magnificent example of British engineering and design. SHADOW FACTORIES AND THE SUPERMARINE AVIATION WORKS Reginald J Mitchell, designer of the legendary Spitfire was Chief Engineer at Supermarine Aviation Works in Woolston, Southampton. His inspired ‘seaplanes’ were designed with liquid-cooled engines and stream-lined bodies, with low drag. It was Mitchell’s Supermarine S6B that won the prestigious and sought after Schneider Trophy in 1931 and was clearly the precursor to his iconic masterpiece, the Spitfire in 1936. The Air Ministry quickly recognised that Mitchell’s Spitfire was both robust and adaptable and began ordering from Supermarine in earnest. The threat of Nazi Germany, the Battle of France and subsequent evacuation of Dunkirk saw Spitfire production rapidly multiply. But it was during the summer of 1940 that the south coast of England came under intense bombing by Germany’s Luftwaffe. It wasn’t long before the Supermarine Aviation Works was targeted and manufacture was disrupted by continual air raids. The intense need to keep up production of this most precious fighter led the Air Ministry to help Supermarine set up shadow factories on the south coast and beyond. These shadow factories were workshops, garages, sheds, bus depots and even a hotel, and were predominantly filled with unqualified women, girls and boys. Supermarine and its army of workers produced over 2000 Spitfires during the summer of 1940. It was through this unquenchable spirit that the Battle of Britain was won. Top Secret, the mission, codenamed Ramrod 564 , would rely on precision bombing to blow the high prison walls and free 120 French resistance patriots due to be executed. The mission was urgent, the executions were imminent. RAF Second Tactical Air Force (2TAF) under Air Vice Marshall Basil Embry were tasked with creating a plan in just 8 days. His plan aimed to breach the high walls in two places, destroy the guardhouse and blow the prison at both ends. To succeed the operation would need three things: pilots skilled in low-level daylight bombing, aircraft designed for speed and manoeuvrability, and an exceptional leader. The de Havilland Mosquito DH.98 FB Mk VI was the plane of choice. A fighter-bomber, fast, light and proven for surprise intruder strike attacks. The mission leader was Group Captain ‘Pick’ Pickard DSO DFC. A national hero, who at just 28 years old had received the DSO three times. Greatly experienced, he had a reputation for being composed under fire. He would lead the pilots of 140 Wing. Carefully chosen, they comprised of Mosquitos flown by New Zealand, Australian and British personnel from 487 Squadron (RNZAF), 464 Squadron (RAAF) and 21 Squadron (RAF). The Amiens Prison raid was an extremely difficult mission. They needed to fly nearly 100 miles across the English Channel at just 50ft above the water, to remain undetected by radar. They also needed great speed (250 mph) as just a few miles from the prison, the German Luftwaffe held a crack squadron of Focke-Wulf Fw 190 fighter planes. On 18 th February 1944 a storm was brewing on the northern coast of France. The blizzard reached England, creating almost impossible flying conditions, but this was a life-or-death mission and Pickard’s team agreed to take the chance. 19 Mosquitos took off into the storm, staggered in 3 waves of six, with a photo reconnaissance Mosquito to record the attack. watches.description: Technical Design Attributes Latitude and Longitude reference Daytona Beach Date code references the Sunbeam land speed record 1920’s period dial and hand design Exhibition watch back with custom rotor Matt silver stopwatch cradle emulates vintage dashboard fixing Case 44mm diameter body in 316L stainless steel billet and finished in matt silver with straight barrel knurl and brushed top chamfer Backplate and lugs are billet machined from a single piece of 316L stainless steel and matt finished. Winding Crown and Pushers Main Crown: Screw lock & sprung oversize straight diamond knurled and dome topped crown in polished 316L stainless steel with triple seal technology Chronograph Pushers: Sprung & double sealed pusher at 11 o’ clock (start/stop red polished) & 1 o’clock (reset silver polished) Crystals Front: Custom double curved domed sapphire glass with blue AR coating on the internal surface Movement Valjoux 7750 (decorated with custom rotor) 28,800vph 25 jewels Self-winding ball bearing rotor Power reserve ~48 hours Water resistance: 10ATM (100m) 100% tested Dial Black enamel over brass substrate with over printed vintage dial numerals highlighted in Super Luminova X1 luminous pigment Sweep seconds sub-dial & minute & hour Chronograph sub-dials Steel satin dial ring with 0.2 second resolution indexes Hands Matt steel with inset SuperLuminova X1 luminous pigment Red Chronograph function hands Dimensions 44mm diameter 15.7mm thick 22mm lug width 52.5mm lug to lug pin spacing Weight 150g including strap Strap 22/20mm Zero West custom Military and aerospace grade cross-linked fluoroelastomer rubber. 1 fixed and 1 sliding keeper Reverse sculptured relief Matt finish Matt silver stainless steel buckle with engraved ZW logo THE RECORD THE CAR THE RECORD Ever since the first motorcar took to the road, man has wanted to make it go faster. It’s a human trait, a lust for adrenaline, a thirst for competition. This compulsion to race cars has taken many forms but the ultimate goal is to be the fastest person on Earth, whether that was is in the air, on water or land. The 1920’s saw great international competition in land-speed record attempts. The mechanised world was developing fast after the horrors of WW1 which included the advancement of the internal combustion engine and the motor industry and a fierce international rivalry existed for holding the much coveted land-speed record. During the 1920’s the land-speed goal was to break the 200mph barrier and during that decade, the land-speed record was broken no fewer than eleven times. THE CAR The elusive 200mph barrier was finally broken on 29th March 1927 at Daytona Beach, USA, by an Englishman called Sir Henry Segrave, driving a British built Sunbeam car called “Mystery” aka Sunbeam 1000 hp. The speed recorded was 203.79 mph. It was an incredible car built by the British Sunbeam Motorcar Company of Wolverhampton. A colossus at 24ft long, 8ft wide and weighing in at 4 tons it was clad in aluminium alloy and painted in a bright red livery. Two 22.4 litre V12 Sunbeam Matabele aero engines, synchronised and mounted in tandem powered the car, one in front and one behind the driver cockpit. Transmission was via a 3 speed gearbox, its final stage being twin chain direct drive to the rear wheels. The record would not stand for long and was broken in February of the following year by another Englishman, Sir Malcolm Campbell, at a speed of 206.956 mph. Seagrave however went on to retain the record again in 1929 in a car called Golden Arrow at a speed of 231.446 mph, and once again Britain’s dominance in leading the world in engineering and setting new land speed records was upheld. Born in Shoreham-by-Sea in 1891, Scott-Paine would go on to forge an illustrious career which would see him mastermind the creation of the Supermarine Aviation Company as well as the first cross-Channel flying-boat service, the British Power Boat Company and Imperial Airways. He was a thrill seeker and with his Supermarine aircraft company, won the coveted 1922 Schneider Seaplane Trophy. Not satisfied with sitting back on the Schneider Trophy success, Scott-Paine turned his attention to his love of the water by designing a groundbreaking hydroplane boat. The project was cloaked in secrecy at his Hythe based British Power Boat Company and within just ten weeks, the iconic world record breaking single engined craft named Miss Britain III was launched. THE HYDROPLANE BOAT The 1933 single engined hydroplane was designed by Scott-Paine and Fred Cooper to challenge for the International Harmsworth Trophy. It was a revolutionary design with aluminium reinforced wooden stringers and a highly polished Alclad pure aluminium skin and because of its groundbreaking geometry and lightweight materials, it weighed in at just 1.5 tons. Powered by a 1350 horsepower Napier Lion engine, and with a specially designed propeller, Miss Britain III was able to travel in excess of 100mph. THE RECORD In September 1933 Scott-Paine piloted Miss Britain III in the Harmsworth Trophy challenge. He was narrowly beaten in a thrilling contest by Miss America X, a 38ft four engined, 7,800 horsepower colossus of a boat. The racing was close and the losing margin less than 1.5mph, but despite his defeat, Scott-Paine was lauded a British hero in what was described by the press as a “David vs Goliath” contest. Just two months later on 16th November 1933 on Southampton Water, Scott-Paine set a new world water speed record in Miss Britain III, being the first single engined speedboat to exceed 100mph. A record that remarkably stood until the 1980’s. TIME: 16/11/1933 – PLACE: 50.845°N 1.328°W

watches.description: “At the core of our brand is a defining line. the main line of longitude; The prime meridian. In essence, to pinpoint your position on Earth you need two coordinates: latitude & longitude. Latitude, or the north/south coordinate, at that time could be precisely fixed by observing the stars. To position yourself east/west on the globe you need to know your longitude but this coordinate cannot be calculated from the stars. It can however be established by measuring the accurate period of time from a known fixed reference point, but before the 18th century no timepiece existed that was accurate enough to navigate by. MARINE TIMING In 1714 the British government set up the Longitude Act to reward anyone who could practically solve the accurate positioning of longitude, and a pioneering British horologist called John Harrison developed designs throughout the 1700’s to refine and innovate accurate clock and watch mechanisms. This culminated in his H4 marine chronometer design that had a highly complex movement, at the heart of which was a vertical escapement. This British designed marine chronometer set the benchmark which finally enabled the accurate positioning of longitude. By the 19th century, marine chronometers were the most accurate way of calculating longitude and in 1884, 22 countries decided by committee to standardise and fix the location of the prime meridian. This line of zero longitude was designated to pass through the Royal Observatory at Greenwich in London and so the navigational reference of time was born, but it was the tenacity and pioneering designs of the great John Harrison that enabled this momentous feat TIME: 22/10/1884 – PLACE: 51.48°N – 0.00°W

It was here he became an ‘Airman’ in name and began training to be a pilot at Prestwick in Scotland. Called into active service on 1 st September 1939, the same day that Nazi Germany invaded Poland and initiated WW2, Girdwood entered Flight Training School to polish his technique and fine tune his skills. Posted to RAF Hendon on the 17 th May 1940, where the historic 257 Squadron was about to reform, he was one of the first arrivals alongside two other freshly trained Sergeant Pilots. 257 Squadron was battle ready with Hawker Hurricanes and fully operational by the 1 st July and Sergeant Pilot Alexander ‘Jock’ Girdwood would enter the Battle of Britain confident of his ability and the valiant ‘Few’ beside him. HURRICANE P3708 Hurricane P3708 was manufactured at Hawker Aircraft Ltd at Langley near Slough. This now legendary plane was an early Mk 1 Hurricane, designed by influential aeronautical engineer Sydney Camm. His clean single seat fighter, The Hurricane , was created after discussions with the Air Ministry regarding an increasingly urgent need for a mono-wing fighter plane. After trials, the initial design was quickly updated from fabric skinned wings to metal and armoured plating in front of the cockpit and an armoured windscreen. It was designed for rapid engagement with enemy fighters and could outgun them with 8 remotely operated wing mounted 0.303 Browning machine guns. Powered by a Rolls-Royce Merlin engine, the Mk 1 had a top speed of 324 mph at 15 600ft. Camm’s design was simple but effective: the Hurricane could be manufactured quickly and was straight forward to maintain, its ease of handling and stable gun platform ensured it was adored by pilots and engineers alike. After a successful test flight at Langley Airfield, P3708 was released to RAF No. 15 Maintenance Unit at Wrougton in Wiltshire on 22 nd May 1940. With the MU it was designated as a reserve aircraft before becoming closely acquainted with 257 Squadron and Sgt Pilot Alexander Girdwood at RAF Hendon as they entered The Battle of Britain . A legendary icon of British design and engineering, a locomotive that evokes nostalgia for the romance of a bygone era of steam travel. This is everything that we at Zero West are passionate about and the inspiration we search for behind every timepiece. When the National Railway Museum, part of the Science Museum Group approached us in 2022 explaining that they were looking for partners to mark the 100th anniversary of Flying Scotsman, we were intrigued. As one of the world’s most famous locomotives, with pioneering designer and a world record for speed, Flying Scotsman was the perfect fit for us. Designed alongside the ‘Mallard’ by Sir Nigel Gresley, Flying Scotsman was built in Doncaster, the first locomotive of the newly formed London and North Eastern Railway (LNER). It went into service on 24 February 1923 with number 1472, as part of the A1 class which were the most powerful locomotives used by the LNER at that time. DESIGN Our Flying Scotsman watches showcase new 41mm models which retain the iconic ZW house style of a billet machined head integrated to our unique DSL lug configuration, and are a new design. The watch head has a 13.1mm profile and is unique in showcasing a piece of steel used on Flying Scotsman in its large exhibition back. Through our collaboration with the National Railway Museum, part of the Science Museum Group, we obtained some steel boiler tube which had been removed during a scheduled refit of the Scotsman’s powerful steam boiler. The tube was then carefully slit and flattened into a rough rectangular sheet for fly-cutting to an exact thickness on the milling machine. Secrecy was such that very few people outside the squadron knew where they were going or what they were about to do. On a hillside overlooking the target, there was a church with a very menacing steeple which left only seconds to pull-up after releasing the bomb. Without longitude, ships could be hundreds of miles from where their crews believed them to be — sometimes with catastrophic consequences. THE LONGITUDE ACT The need for a practical solution became a national priority. In 1714, Parliament passed the Longitude Act, offering substantial financial rewards for a method capable of determining longitude accurately at sea. The challenge would attract some of the greatest scientific minds of the age. JOHN HARRISON The man who ultimately transformed the problem was not an astronomer but a self-taught clockmaker and carpenter born in Yorkshire. John Harrison believed longitude could be solved mechanically: build a timekeeper sufficiently accurate to carry the time at a known location throughout a long ocean voyage. TIME BECOMES POSITION The principle was beautifully simple. Compare local time, established from the sun, with the time carried aboard ship from a known reference point. Every hour of difference represented fifteen degrees of longitude. The problem was creating a mechanical timekeeper accurate enough to make the calculation reliable. H1, H2 & H3 Harrison devoted decades to the challenge. His first three marine timekeepers were extraordinary machines, introducing solutions for temperature, friction and the constant movement of a ship. Each advanced his understanding, but none would become the final answer he was searching for. H4 Completed in 1759, Harrison’s fourth marine timekeeper was radically different. Resembling an oversized pocket watch, H4 used a fast-beating balance and represented the culmination of decades of experimentation. Its successful sea trials demonstrated that accurate portable timekeeping could finally provide a practical solution to longitude. Its design draws on the purposeful clarity of the aircraft’s cockpit, translating the instruments and controls of a 1930s fighter into a contemporary mechanical watch. The black dial takes its cues from the Smiths cockpit clock, with period numerals, highly legible avionic hands and a red-tipped sweep seconds hand. The dial reinterprets the clock’s strong graphic character, while coordinates locate Doncaster Works, where Sir Nigel Gresley’s locomotive was designed and built. The result deliberately feels part watch, part railway instrument — connecting time, place and the golden age of express travel. On the reverse sits the most important detail: an individual disc made from steel boiler tube removed from Flying Scotsman itself. Reworked by Zero West while preserving its working patina, the material carries the physical evidence of thousands of hours spent powering the world’s most famous steam locomotive. @media(max-width:600px){#s6ec{height:0!important}} 02 THE HISTORY SIR NIGEL GRESLEY One of Britain’s greatest railway engineers, Sir Nigel Gresley became Chief Mechanical Engineer of the newly formed LNER in 1923. His locomotives combined power, efficiency and elegance, culminating in machines that would become synonymous with the golden age of British steam. BUILT AT DONCASTER Flying Scotsman emerged from Doncaster Works in 1923 as an A1 Pacific locomotive, originally numbered 1472. Built to Gresley’s design for the newly formed LNER, it entered service on 24 February — beginning a working life that would ultimately span more than a century. LONDON TO EDINBURGH In 1928, Flying Scotsman hauled the inaugural non-stop London to Edinburgh service, completing the 392-mile journey without stopping. A corridor connection to the tender allowed crews to change while travelling, making one of Britain’s great railway journeys possible without interruption. THE MAGIC 100 On 30 November 1934, Flying Scotsman became the first steam locomotive officially authenticated at 100mph. The achievement established its place in railway history and turned Gresley’s locomotive into an international symbol of British speed, engineering and technological ambition. AN EVOLVING MACHINE Flying Scotsman did not remain unchanged. Originally built as an A1, it was progressively improved and rebuilt to Gresley’s more powerful A3 specification, receiving a higher-pressure boiler and other developments that increased efficiency and performance throughout its long working life. A NATIONAL ICON Withdrawn from regular service in 1963, Flying Scotsman escaped the fate of many steam locomotives and entered preservation. It subsequently travelled internationally, including tours of the United States and Australia, becoming one of the most widely recognised steam locomotives in the world. A decade-long £4.2 million restoration followed, returning the locomotive to the main line in 2016 and ensuring its survival as a working piece of British engineering history. 100 YEARS OF FLYING SCOTSMAN On 24 February 2023, Flying Scotsman celebrated 100 years since entering service. It acknowledges the enduring legend created by The Great Escape while keeping the watch firmly rooted in documented history. McQueen’s Triumph motorcycle contributes its sense of mechanical purity, rebellion and function-led design, while the clarity of Spitfire avionics informs a visual language built around necessity and readability. Our hands-on involvement in restoring AA810 completes that connection, uniting authentic provenance, recovered material and purposeful engineering within a watch that preserves the truth of the story rather than merely borrowing its imagery. The S5e interprets the classic Dirty Dozen field watch through small seconds at six, military stencil typography, a countdown quadrant and avionics-framed luminous hands. A concealed message on the sapphire caseback completes the escape narrative. @media(max-width:600px){#ie8c{height:0!important}} 02 THE HISTORY The extraordinary true story connecting a daring pilot, a blue Spitfire, an audacious tunnel escape and the Hollywood classic The Great Escape. SANDY GUNN Alastair “Sandy” Gunn was a young Scottish engineer and RAF Volunteer Reserve pilot. Selected for his navigational ability, he joined the Photographic Reconnaissance Unit and began flying solitary intelligence missions deep into enemy-held territory. PHOTOGRAPHIC RECONNAISSANCE PRU pilots fought with information rather than weapons. Their Spitfires carried cameras instead of guns and depended on speed, altitude and skilful flying to survive while photographing enemy ships, ports, airfields and military installations. SPITFIRE AA810 AA810 was a rare photographic-reconnaissance Spitfire finished in the PRU’s distinctive blue. Built for speed and range, it flew without armament or armour, carrying cameras into places conventional reconnaissance aircraft could not safely reach. THE FINAL MISSION On 5 March 1942, Gunn departed RAF Wick alone to photograph the German battleship Tirpitz in occupied Norway. AA810 was intercepted and shot down, but Gunn survived the crash and was taken prisoner. TUNNEL HARRY Sent to Stalag Luft III, Gunn became part of the organisation behind Tunnel Harry. He was one of 76 men who escaped in March 1944, but was recaptured and murdered on Hitler’s orders—one of the 50. FACT BECOMES FILM Paul Brickhill’s 1950 book brought the mass escape to a wider audience. Producer-director John Sturges adapted it into the 1963 film The Great Escape, dramatising the operation and turning a remarkable wartime episode into enduring popular history. THE MCQUEEN EFFECT Steve McQueen’s fictional Captain Hilts gave the film its rebellious icon: the Cooler King, his motorcycle and the attempted leap to freedom. The role did not portray Gunn, but helped immortalise the escape for generations. AA810 RETURNS After 76 years in the Norwegian mountains, the wreckage of AA810 was recovered for restoration. Zero West sponsored the reconstruction of its instrument panel, creating a direct connection with the aircraft and the inspiration for the S5e and S6e. THE TANGIBLE LINK A small quantity of metal recovered from AA810’s Merlin engine is carefully recast into numbered components fitted to each watch. Rare and historically significant, these pieces forge a tangible link between Gunn, the aircraft, the escape and the story immortalised on film. AA

Its design combines the character of vintage aviation instruments with details taken directly from the mission. A textured black dial, applied three-dimensional numerals and vintage brass-toned hands create the clarity and warmth of a period cockpit instrument. The crown takes its form from an aircraft joystick firing button, while the dial records the coordinates of Amiens Prison and the date of the raid. Turn the watch over and the connection becomes physical. Beneath the rear sapphire crystal sits a precision-cut steel disc taken from the Rolls-Royce Merlin crankshaft of Mosquito HX909 — transforming surviving material from the aircraft into an integral part of the M1. @media(max-width:600px){#d2ba{height:0!important}} 02 THE HISTORY THE WOODEN WONDER The de Havilland Mosquito challenged conventional thinking. Largely constructed from wood and originally conceived without defensive armament, it would rely instead upon exceptional speed. First flown in November 1940, the radical design became one of the most versatile aircraft of the Second World War. SPEED OVER FIREPOWER De Havilland believed that removing the weight and drag of defensive gun turrets could create a bomber fast enough to outrun enemy fighters. Its lightweight wooden construction and twin Rolls-Royce Merlin engines produced an aircraft of extraordinary performance, agility and range. OPERATION JERICHO On 18 February 1944, RAF Mosquitos set out on one of their most audacious missions: a precision, low-level attack on Amiens Prison in occupied France. Codenamed Operation Jericho, the objective was to breach the prison walls and enable prisoners to escape. FIFTY FEET ABOVE THE GROUND Flying beneath German radar demanded extraordinary skill. The Mosquitos crossed the Channel at extremely low level before racing across snow-covered northern France, using roads, villages and other landmarks for navigation as they converged on the prison at precisely the planned time. MOSQUITO HX909 Among the first wave was Mosquito FB Mk VI HX909, flown by New Zealand pilot Merv Darrall with navigator Fred Stevenson. Carrying four 500lb bombs, they approached Amiens at low level before releasing their weapons against the prison’s outer walls. THE WALL IS BREACHED HX909’s attack struck the north wall, blasting a breach through the masonry. Other Mosquitos attacked the walls and guardhouse as prisoners began escaping through the openings. The precision demanded from the crews made Operation Jericho one of the Mosquito’s most famous low-level attacks. THE COST The mission came at a heavy price. Aircraft and aircrew were lost, including the raid’s celebrated leader, Group Captain Percy “Pick” Pickard. Prisoners were also killed during the bombing. Operation Jericho succeeded in creating escape routes, but its human cost remains part of its complex history. A PIECE OF HX909 Unlike most wartime aircraft, the Mosquito’s structure was predominantly wooden, making surviving original material particularly scarce. Steel from the Rolls-Royce Merlin crankshaft that powered HX909 survived — material now precision-cut and incorporated into the M1, physically connecting each watch with the aircraft and its mission. 03 M1 (44mm) GALLERY Showcasing Merlin engine steel, cut from the crankshaft of Mosquito fighter-bomber HX909 04 M1 SPECIFICATION DESIGN ATT

MOSQUITO HX909 Among the first wave was Mosquito FB Mk VI HX909, flown by New Zealand pilot Merv Darrall with navigator Fred Stevenson. Carrying four 500lb bombs, they approached Amiens at low level before releasing their weapons against the prison’s outer walls. THE WALL IS BREACHED HX909’s attack struck the north wall, blasting a breach through the masonry. Other Mosquitos attacked the walls and guardhouse as prisoners began escaping through the openings. The precision demanded from the crews made Operation Jericho one of the Mosquito’s most famous low-level attacks. THE COST The mission came at a heavy price. Aircraft and aircrew were lost, including the raid’s celebrated leader, Group Captain Percy “Pick” Pickard. Prisoners were also killed during the bombing. Operation Jericho succeeded in creating escape routes, but its human cost remains part of its complex history. A PIECE OF HX909 Unlike most wartime aircraft, the Mosquito’s structure was predominantly wooden, making surviving original material particularly scarce. Steel from the Rolls-Royce Merlin crankshaft that powered HX909 survived — material now precision-cut and incorporated into the M1, physically connecting each watch with the aircraft and its mission. 03 M1 (41mm) GALLERY Showcasing Merlin engine steel, cut from the crankshaft of Mosquito fighter-bomber HX909 04 M1 SPECIFICATION DESIGN ATT

watches.description: @media(max-width:1024px){#j8bf{height:1.5rem!important}} WHAT CONNECTS A VULCAN BOMBER, AN 8,000-MILE MISSION, A FALKLANDS RUNWAY AND A MISSION WATCH? MODEL: AV1 MISSION WATCH Dossier: ZW-080 Operation Black Buck Date: 30/04/1982 Coords: 51.4115S – 57.4644E Size: 42mm Material: Aluminium wing metal from XM607 Edition: Limited to 300 pieces Build: Order and dispatched within 4 weeks @media(max-width:1024px){#x429{height:1.5rem!important}} 01 INSPIRATION & DESIGN The AV1 Vulcan draws its inspiration from Avro Vulcan XM607 and its extraordinary role in Operation Black Buck. Its design combines the purposeful language of Cold War aviation with the mission details of the aircraft’s historic 1982 flight from Ascension Island to the Falkland Islands. The black dial takes its cues from Vulcan cockpit instrumentation, with oversized luminous numerals, sword hands and recessed chronograph registers creating the clarity of a military flight instrument. Coordinates, date coding and mission markings reference the target at Port Stanley and Black Buck One. At its heart is a direct connection to XM607 itself. Aluminium recovered from the aircraft’s wing elevon has been machined by Zero West into the dial chapter ring. Rather than simply commemorating the aircraft, the AV1 Vulcan carries an original part of it forward in a new mechanical form. @media(max-width:600px){#c61d{height:0!important}} 02 THE HISTORY THE AVRO VULCAN Designed as a high-altitude nuclear bomber at the beginning of the Cold War, the Avro Vulcan became one of the most distinctive aircraft ever operated by the RAF. Its enormous delta wing, four Olympus engines and unmistakable silhouette made it an icon of British aviation. A VERY DIFFERENT WAR When Argentine forces invaded the Falkland Islands in April 1982, the Vulcan was approaching retirement. An aircraft conceived to carry Britain’s nuclear deterrent suddenly faced an entirely different challenge: delivering conventional weapons against targets almost 4,000 miles from the nearest suitable British airfield. OPERATION BLACK BUCK The RAF devised an extraordinarily complex plan. Vulcans would fly from Wideawake Airfield on Ascension Island to the Falklands, attack Argentine positions around Port Stanley and return. Reaching the target required a carefully choreographed relay of Victor tankers refuelling both the bomber and each other. XM607 Two Vulcans departed Ascension for Black Buck One on the night of 30 April 1982. XM607 was initially the reserve aircraft, but when the primary Vulcan was forced to turn back, Squadron Leader Martin Withers and his crew inherited the mission and continued south towards the Falklands. THE LONG FLIGHT SOUTH XM607 crossed thousands of miles of empty South Atlantic, receiving fuel seven times during the mission. Navigation, fuel calculations and the Victor tanker operation had to work together with extraordinary precision. Failure at a critical point could leave the Vulcan without enough fuel to return. PORT STANLEY Early on 1 May, XM607 approached Port Stanley airfield carrying twenty-one 1,000lb bombs. The aircraft crossed the runway diagonally and released its entire load in sequence. One bomb struck the runway, while others damaged the surrounding airfield and demonstrated Britain’s ability to strike the islands from extreme range. THE LONGEST-RANGE RAID XM607 returned safely to Ascension after 15 hours and 45 minutes in the air. At the time, Black Buck One was the longest-range bombing operation conducted under combat conditions — an extraordinary mission involving the Vulcan, Victor tankers and crews operating close to the limits of their aircraft. XM607 LIVES ON The Vulcan fleet retired shortly after the Falklands war, but XM607 survived. Today the aircraft is preserved at RAF Waddington, permanently associated with Black Buck One and one of the most ambitious long-range air operations ever attempted by the Royal Air Force. 03 AV1 GALLERY 04 AV1 SPECIFICATION DESIGN ATTRIBUTES

watches.description: @media(max-width:1024px){#y8fe{height:1.5rem!important}} WHAT CONNECTS A SPITFIRE PILOT, TUNNEL HARRY, A MIDNIGHT BREAKOUT AND A AVIATION CHRONOGRAPH? MODEL: S6E FIELD WATCH Dossier: ZW-050 Great Escape Spitfire Date: 24/03/1944 Coords: 51.5986N – 15.3075E Size: 42mm Material: Merlin Engine metal from AA810 Edition: Limited to 100 pieces Build: Order and dispatched within 4 weeks @media(max-width:1024px){#kb9d{height:1.5rem!important}} 01 INSPIRATION & DESIGN The design draws together Sandy Gunn’s courage, determination and tragic fate with the ingenuity and disciplined engineering behind Tunnel Harry. It acknowledges the enduring legend created by The Great Escape while keeping the watch firmly rooted in documented history. McQueen’s Triumph motorcycle contributes its sense of mechanical purity, rebellion and function-led design, while the clarity of Spitfire avionics informs a visual language built around necessity and readability. Our hands-on involvement in restoring AA810 completes that connection, uniting authentic provenance, recovered material and purposeful engineering within a watch that preserves the truth of the story rather than merely borrowing its imagery. The S6e draws inspiration from Spitfire AA810’s airspeed indicator, combining a distinctive chronograph layout with luminous hands and aviation-inspired detailing. A concealed message on the sapphire caseback completes the escape narrative. @media(max-width:600px){#x01c{height:0!important}} 02 THE HISTORY The extraordinary true story connecting a daring pilot, a blue Spitfire, an audacious tunnel escape and the Hollywood classic The Great Escape. SANDY GUNN Alastair “Sandy” Gunn was a young Scottish engineer and RAF Volunteer Reserve pilot. Selected for his navigational ability, he joined the Photographic Reconnaissance Unit and began flying solitary intelligence missions deep into enemy-held territory. PHOTOGRAPHIC RECONNAISSANCE PRU pilots fought with information rather than weapons. Their Spitfires carried cameras instead of guns and depended on speed, altitude and skilful flying to survive while photographing enemy ships, ports, airfields and military installations. SPITFIRE AA810 AA810 was a rare photographic-reconnaissance Spitfire finished in the PRU’s distinctive blue. Built for speed and range, it flew without armament or armour, carrying cameras into places conventional reconnaissance aircraft could not safely reach. THE FINAL MISSION On 5 March 1942, Gunn departed RAF Wick alone to photograph the German battleship Tirpitz in occupied Norway. AA810 was intercepted and shot down, but Gunn survived the crash and was taken prisoner. TUNNEL HARRY Sent to Stalag Luft III, Gunn became part of the organisation behind Tunnel Harry. He was one of 76 men who escaped in March 1944, but was recaptured and murdered on Hitler’s orders—one of the 50. FACT BECOMES FILM Paul Brickhill’s 1950 book brought the mass escape to a wider audience. Producer-director John Sturges adapted it into the 1963 film The Great Escape, dramatising the operation and turning a remarkable wartime episode into enduring popular history. THE MCQUEEN EFFECT Steve McQueen’s fictional Captain Hilts gave the film its rebellious icon: the Cooler King, his motorcycle and the attempted leap to freedom. The role did not portray Gunn, but helped immortalise the escape for generations. AA810 RETURNS After 76 years in the Norwegian mountains, the wreckage of AA810 was recovered for restoration. Zero West sponsored the reconstruction of its instrument panel, creating a direct connection with the aircraft and the inspiration for the S5e and S6e. THE TANGIBLE LINK A small quantity of metal recovered from AA810’s Merlin engine is carefully recast into numbered components fitted to each watch. Rare and historically significant, these pieces forge a tangible link between Gunn, the aircraft, the escape and the story immortalised on film. 03 S6E GALLERY 04 S6E SPECIFICATION DESIGN ATTRIBUTES Latitude &
